## The idea

Many choices are about *where* an alternative sits rather than how much of something it offers: how sweet a chocolate bar, how far left or right a candidate, how formal a restaurant. In a spatial model, each person has an ideal point and prefers alternatives closer to it. Harold Hotelling used the idea for two shops on a street; Anthony Downs applied it to elections.

The striking prediction in one dimension is convergence. Each candidate wins the voters on their side of the midpoint between them, so a candidate gains by moving toward the opponent, and both end up at the position of the *median voter*. That explains why many two-party elections are close and fought over the centre. With several dimensions the logic breaks down: for almost any position there is another that a majority prefers, so there need be no stable platform at all, and whoever controls the agenda or defends the status quo gains power.

## Formulation

::: {.model-box}
**Setup.** An alternative is a point $\vec a = (a_1, \dots, a_N)$ in an $N$-dimensional attribute space; each individual has an ideal point $\vec x = (x_1, \dots, x_N)$.

**Payoff.** An individual's utility from an alternative falls with squared distance from the ideal point:

$$
\pi(\vec x, \vec a) = C - (x_1 - a_1)^2 - (x_2 - a_2)^2 - \dots - (x_N - a_N)^2 ,
$$

so each individual chooses the nearest alternative.

**Results.** In one dimension with two competitors seeking the most support, the unique equilibrium is for both to locate at the median ideal point (the median voter theorem). In two or more dimensions, a position that beats every other in a pairwise majority vote exists only under special symmetry conditions, so generally no equilibrium exists.
:::

For example, with ideal point $\vec x = (3, 4, 6)$, alternative $\vec a = (2, 1, 8)$ and $C = 20$, the payoff is $20 - 1 - 9 - 4 = 6$.

## Interactive model

Two thousand voters with ideal points from 0 to 10, and two candidates. The histogram colours each voter by the candidate they prefer. Move the candidates by hand, then look at the lower chart: starting from your positions, each candidate in turn moves to the position that wins the most votes against the other, and both converge on the median voter, even when the electorate is polarized.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {rng, range, median, C, fmt, pct} from "../js/models.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof shape = Inputs.radio(["Centred", "Skewed", "Polarized (two camps)"], {value: "Polarized (two camps)", label: "Electorate"})
viewof posA = Inputs.range([0, 10], {value: 2, step: 0.1, label: "Candidate A's position"})
viewof posB = Inputs.range([0, 10], {value: 8.5, step: 0.1, label: "Candidate B's position"})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 38, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
```

```{ojs}
spatial = {
  const r = rng(seed), clip = v => Math.min(10, Math.max(0, v));
  const voters = range(2000).map(() => clip(
    shape === "Centred" ? r.normal(5, 1.6) : shape === "Skewed" ? 1 + r.gamma(2, 1.3) : (r() < 0.55 ? r.normal(3, 1) : r.normal(7.5, 1))));
  const share = (a, b) => {
    if (a === b) return 0.5;
    let n = 0;
    for (const v of voters) { const da = Math.abs(v - a), db = Math.abs(v - b); n += da < db ? 1 : da === db ? 0.5 : 0; }
    return n / voters.length;
  };
  const grid = range(101).map(i => i / 10);
  const best = other => grid.reduce((b, x) => (share(x, other) > share(b, other) + 1e-12 ? x : b), grid[0]);
  let a = posA, b = posB;
  const path = [{round: 0, a, b}];
  for (let k = 1; k <= 120; k++) {
    if (k % 2) a = best(b); else b = best(a);
    path.push({round: k, a, b});
    if (k > 4 && Math.abs(a - b) <= 0.21 && Math.abs((a + b) / 2 - path[k - 4].a / 2 - path[k - 4].b / 2) < 0.11) break;
  }
  return {voters, med: median(voters), shareA: share(posA, posB), path};
}
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  ariaLabel: "Spatial Competition Model: voters and candidates",
  ariaDescription: "Horizontal axis: ideal point from 0 to 10. Vertical axis: number of voters. Bars are coloured by the candidate each voter prefers (teal for A, orange for B). Labelled vertical lines mark the candidates and the dashed line the median voter. The summary below the charts states the result in words.",
  height: 230,
  x: {label: "Ideal point", domain: [0, 10]},

    Plot.rectY(spatial.voters, Plot.binX({y: "count"}, {x: d => d, fill: d => (Math.abs(d - posA) <= Math.abs(d - posB) ? C.teal : C.orange), thresholds: 50, domain: [0, 10]})),
    Plot.ruleX([spatial.med], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "4 3"}),

    Plot.text([{x: posA, t: "A"}, {x: posB, t: "B"}], {x: "x", text: "t", frameAnchor: "top", dy: -4, fontWeight: "bold", fill: "currentColor"})
  ]
})
```

  const voters = range(2000).map(() => clip(
    shape === "Centred" ? r.normal(5, 1.6) : shape === "Skewed" ? 1 + r.gamma(2, 1.3) : (r() < 0.55 ? r.normal(3, 1) : r.normal(7.5, 1))));

## R {.unlisted}

```{.r}
# Spatial competition: two candidates best-respond and converge to the median.
set.seed(38)
voters <- pmin(10, pmax(0, ifelse(runif(2000) < 0.55,
  rnorm(2000, 3, 1), rnorm(2000, 7.5, 1)
))) # a polarized electorate

share <- function(a, b) {
  if (a == b) {
    return(0.5)
  }
  mean(ifelse(abs(voters - a) < abs(voters - b), 1,
    ifelse(abs(voters - a) == abs(voters - b), 0.5, 0)
  ))
}
grid <- seq(0, 10, by = 0.1)
best <- function(other) grid[which.max(sapply(grid, share, b = other))]

a <- 2
b <- 8.5
cat(sprintf("Starting shares: A %.3f\n", share(a, b)))
for (round in 1:120) { # each best response leapfrogs the rival
  if (round %% 2 == 1) a <- best(b) else b <- best(a)
}
cat(sprintf(
  "After best responses: A at %.1f, B at %.1f; median %.2f\n",
  a, b, median(voters)
))

hist(voters,
  breaks = 50, col = "grey80", border = "white", main = "",
  xlab = "Ideal point"
)
abline(v = c(a, b), col = c("#148a91", "#d95f02"), lwd = 3)
abline(v = median(voters), lty = 2)
```

:::

## Takeaways

::: takeaways
- With one dimension and two competitors, competition pulls both to the median ideal point.
- Convergence explains close elections and similar products, and it happens even when voters are polarized.
- In several dimensions there is usually no unbeatable position, so agenda setters, veto players and the status quo matter.
:::

## Uses

::: uses
- **Predict.** Where parties will position themselves, and that two-party elections will be close.
- **Explain.** Why competing products, stores and policies cluster together, and why multi-issue politics is unstable.
- **Design.** Locate a new product where its *Voronoi neighbourhood* (the people it is closest to) is large, rather than at the crowded centre.
:::

## Related models

- [Hedonic Competition Model](hedonic-competition.qmd): attributes where more is better, rather than where each person has an ideal.
- [Shapley–Shubik Index](shapley-shubik-index.qmd): power in voting bodies.
- [Zero-Sum Games](zero-sum-games.qmd): electoral competition between two candidates is zero-sum.
